A region, perhaps in Arabia, known for its pure gold (1 Kin. 9:28; Job 22:24).

**Havilah.** See note on 2:11 and 10:7. The name Havilah was probably used of two different locations.
Though these locations are unidentified, the names of the sons of Joktan point to a location in southern Arabia.

See note on 10:1–11:9. Some scholars identify the tower in this narrative as the three-hundred-foot high temple ziggurat of Marduk at Babylon. In Hebrew the name for Babylon is _Babel_. The same arrogant pride that inspired rebellious Eve and Adam to rival God’s knowledge (3:5) and the ungodly Cain to build his city (4:17), now inspires “the whole earth” (v. 4). The mention of “Shinar” (v. 2; cf. 10:10) and “Babel” (v. 9; cf. 10:10) recall Nimrod’s rebellious kingdom (10:8–12 and notes).

**11:1 whole earth.** See note on 10:1–11:9.

See notes on 4:17; 8:1–12:9; and 10:10.

**tower ... in the heavens.** This description suggests a monumental effort motivated by pride (cf. Is. 2:15–17). Human beings—this time in a titanic attempt at corporate self-assertion—again sacrilegiously challenge God (3:6 note).

**make a name for ourselves.** Since “name” connotes fame and progeny, these city builders are attempting to find significance and immortality in their own achievements. But God gives an everlasting name only to those who serve Him (12:2).

**lest we be dispersed.** Like Cain in their isolation from God, these proud sinners fear dislocation and perhaps one another as well (4:14). Also like Cain, they find their solution in a city that rivals God—a strategy that involves disobeying God’s command to “fill the earth” (9:1).

LORD **came down to see.** Divine investigation prior to judgment is frequently depicted in Genesis (3:11–13; 4:9, 10; 18:21). Rather than conflict with the doctrine of divine omniscience (cf. 6:6 note), this anthropomorphic description of God’s activity serves to emphasize that divine judgment is always according to truth. The Mesopotamian ziggurat towers were built as descending stairways for the gods to travel. But God comes down in judgment _on_ this tower of human pride.

verse_quote: the beginning of what they will do.
note: See note on 10:8.
See note on 1:26.

Ironically, instead of attaining significance and immortality, they achieve alienation and dispersal. Expulsion was the earlier fate of Adam and Eve (3:23) and of Cain (4:12). This judgment is also an act of grace; in isolation, the peoples are more likely to turn to God (12:3; Acts 17:26, 27).
An ironic etymology derived from the Hebrew word meaning “confuse.” To the Babylonians, Babel meant “gate of god.”

See note 5:3–32. This linear genealogy continues the line of Seth in 5:3–32. Both genealogies link Abraham to the promised seed of Eve. The present genealogy, which overlaps with the segmented genealogy in 10:21–31, forms a transition from primeval history to the account of Abraham.

As is common in ancient genealogies, it is apparent that this genealogy contains gaps. If it were precisely sequential, the events of chs. 9–11 would cover less than three centuries, all of Abraham’s ancestors would have been still living when he was born, and Shem would outlive Abraham by fourteen years. The purpose of this genealogy is to record the advances of the messianic line (see Introduction: Literary Features).

**11:10 These are the generations of.** See note on 2:4.
In the Sumerian flood story the ages of the kings are also reduced after the flood (5:3–32 note).
See note on 10:21.
See note on 10:25.
See notes on 17:5.

This introduction to the Abraham story identifies the main characters in Abraham’s life: father, brother, wife, sister-in-law, and nephew.

**11:27 these are the generations of Terah.** See note on 2:4. Terah, the father of the principal figure, Abraham, gives his name to the family history, since the family involved in this story descends from him. After this introduction he is not mentioned again, probably because he did not share Abraham’s faith. The family may have been involved in moon worship, since Ur and Haran were important centers for worship of the Mesopotamian moon gods Nanna and Sin (cf. Josh. 24:2).

**Nahor.** See 22:20–24.

Haran’s premature death explains the fate of his children in this closely knit family. Abraham adopted Lot, Haran’s son (v. 31; 12:4), and Nahor married Milcah, Haran’s daughter.

**Ur of the Chaldeans.** Probably the important city in southern Mesopotamia on the Euphrates River (flourished c. 3000–1900 B.C.). Because the Chaldeans did not reach southern Mesopotamia until after the time of Moses (and almost a millennium after Abraham), this description of Ur may represent an updating of the text after the time of Moses (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).
She is the daughter of Terah by a different mother than Abraham’s (20:2). The prohibition against such a marriage was unknown in patriarchal times (cf. Lev. 18:9; 20:17; Deut. 27:22).
This mention of childlessness anticipates the miraculous provision of offspring to continue the covenant line of promise (18:1–15; 21:1–12).

If Abram was born when Terah was seventy years old (v. 26), and if Abram departed Haran when he was seventy-five years old (12:4) after the death of his father Terah (Acts 7:4), Terah is only 145 years old at his death. Several possible solutions to this apparent difficulty have been advanced. Some suggest that Stephen in Acts 7:4 relies on a different Hebrew textual tradition (the Samaritan Pentateuch text of this passage reads “145 years”). Others propose that the Hebrew word rendered “fathered” in v. 26 means “began to father” and that Abram was not the firstborn.

**11:27–22:19** God’s division of the world into nations (11:1–9), following their failed attempt to build a universal city, provides the backdrop for God’s call of Abram. With Abram commences the story of God’s creation of Israel, a story in which He will reveal His freedom in being merciful to Israel, His holiness in judging them, His faithfulness in restoring them, and His absolute sovereignty over human history. Abram’s story begins with his departure from a city of man (Ur) in search of the city “whose designer and builder is God” (Heb. 11:10).

Abraham’s call as an agent of redemptive grace parallels Noah’s as the mediator of a covenant to all creation (8:1–12:9 note). The form of God’s call to Abraham also resembles His pattern in creation (1:3–31 note)—announcement, command (v. 1), and report (vv. 4–9)—but the pattern is broken by the divine promise (vv. 2–3), highlighting Abraham’s faith and believing obedience (vv. 4–9; cf. 22:1–19; Rom. 4:3; Heb. 11:8–12).

**12:1–3** These verses mark a pivotal point in Genesis and in the history of redemption as God begins to establish a covenant people for Himself in fulfillment of the promise He made in 3:15. The progress of God’s redemptive plan is evident in His setting Abraham apart (v. 1) and making Israel into a great nation (v. 2; 46:3). It climaxes in Jesus Christ, the true seed of Abraham (Gal. 3:16), who brings salvation to the world (v. 3). The call to Abraham is passed on to the next two patriarchs, Isaac (26:2–4) and Jacob (28:14). The nation will be formed from Jacob’s twelve sons (ch. 49). See theological note “Covenant” on p. 37.

The call of Abraham requires a response of obedience based on a genuine faith in what God promises. By abandoning the security of his homeland and family, Abraham trusts that God will fulfill His promise to make Abraham into a great nation despite the fact that he is both childless and landless. Moreover, God promises that through Abraham all the families of the earth will enjoy God’s favor, although the beneficiaries will be only those who bless Abraham. What is promised to Abraham at this stage, nationhood and international blessing, will be later guaranteed through distinctive covenants (15:1–21; 17:1–27).

**12:1 said.** The call comes to Abraham in Ur before his father died, not in Haran (15:7).

**the land.** The scope of this land grant will be progressively defined (12:7; 13:14–17; 15:18–21).

Crucial elements of divine blessing and promise in Genesis—fruitfulness and dominion—are evident here and are further spelled out in 22:17.

**make your name great.** What the city builders at Babel sought in their own strength (11:4 note), God gives in sovereign grace. Subsequent history confirms God’s promise—the great names of Abraham and David (2 Sam. 7:9) prefigure that of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:9–11).

**you will be a blessing.** This occurrence of the verb “to bless” is an imperative. Abraham will not only be blessed, but is to be a blessing to others (v. 3).

verse_quote: bless those ... him ... I will curse.
note:
The extent of God’s merciful and gracious intention is indicated in the Hebrew by a switch from the plural object of blessing to the singular object of cursing. The subsequent account of Abraham’s life confirms that many will receive God’s blessing through the unique seed of Abraham (22:18; Gal. 3:8; Rev. 7:9, 10).

**those who bless.** Those who acknowledge Abraham and his offspring as God’s agent of blessing.

**him who dishonors you I will curse.** The Hebrew words here translated “dishonors” and “curse” differ: the second means “to disdain,” while the first often has the sense of “to weaken” (3:14). God will be an effective adversary of those who curse Abraham and his seed.

**in you.** Abraham will play a vital role in the process by which God’s blessing will come to the families of the earth. Later, this will be extended to involve his seed (22:18), eventually coming to fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the seed of Abraham (Gal. 3:16), and in the spiritual seed of Abraham of all ages united with Christ (Gal. 3:29; Phil. 3:3 note). This spiritual seed is not made up of all ethnic Israelites; rather, it includes only believing ethnic Israelites and believing ethnic Gentiles (Rom. 11; Gal. 3:26–28). Those who are not of faith, be they ethnically Jew or Gentile, do not inherit the promises of God (John 8:39; Rom. 9:6–8).

**shall be blessed.** Some have argued that the Hebrew verb should be translated reflexively: “shall bless themselves” (i.e., will desire the blessing of Abraham). While grammatically possible, this proposed reading hardly does justice to the context of this divine promise, and the passive translation here (“be blessed”) presents no real linguistic difficulties. In addition, the Septuagint (Greek OT) rendered it as passive. We are fully justified in viewing this promise as a reference to God’s plan for the salvation of the world.
See note on 11:32.

See 33:18–34:31; 48:22; 50:25; Josh. 24:32 and notes.

**oak of Moreh.** A tree whose greater height made it a preferred place of worship (13:18; 18:1; 21:33). Although pagans worshiped fertility deities under such trees, Abraham, who looked for a heavenly city (Heb. 11:10), worships only the true God (v. 8). The name “Moreh” means “teacher.” This was probably a pagan site for oracles; the Lord sanctified it by appearing to Abraham (v. 7).

**the Canaanites ... in the land.** Two obstacles stand in the way of God’s promise: Sarah’s barrenness (11:30) and the Canaanites who prevent him from settling in the land.

On various occasions God appears to the patriarchs (15:1, 4; 17:1; 18:1; 20:7; 26:2, 24; 28:10–15; 31:3; 35:9; 48:3). Later, He will come to live among their descendants when the tabernacle is constructed (Ex. 40:34–38).

**offspring.** Grammatically, the Hebrew for “offspring” is a collective singular noun, which may denote either one or many depending on the context. Paul declares that it pertains uniquely to Jesus Christ as the source of blessing (Gal. 3:16) and to all those who share Abraham’s faith in God as the recipients of blessing (Rom. 4:16, 23–24; Gal. 3:26–29).

**built there an altar.** By this act the father of the new nation begins the process of consecrating the Promised Land to God (Ex. 20:24; Josh. 22:19). See v. 8; 13:18; 22:9; 26:25; 35:7.

verse_quote: called upon the name of the
note: LORD **.** See 4:26 and note.
The desert region southwest of the Dead Sea. Covering an area of about 4,500 square miles (7240 km), its rainfall is too low to sustain cultivated grain.

The matriarch Sarah is also endangered in ch. 20. Abraham’s exodus from Egypt prefigures the nation’s later exodus: God sends a famine (v. 10; 47:4); the Egyptians afflict them (vv. 12–15; Ex. 1:11–14); God sends plagues on the Egyptians (v. 17; Ex. 8–11); the Egyptians let them go with great wealth (vv. 16, 20; Ex. 12:33–36); they return to the land by stages through the wilderness (13:3; Ex. 17:1); and finally arrive back in the land, where they worship the Lord (13:3; Ex. 15:17). See Ps. 105:14, 15; 1 Cor. 10:1–4.

Although hospitality to strangers was a duty in the ancient Near East (18:2–5; Deut. 10:18, 19), strangers remained vulnerable (cf. 19:3–11). Abraham is not necessarily selling Sarah’s honor to save himself, since this ruse was planned long before (cf. 20:13), perhaps to stall for time in dangerous circumstances (cf. 24:55; 34:13–17). His actions, however, reflect his failure at this point to trust God fully.
See note on 11:29.
The Hebrew here does not necessarily imply sexual intercourse (cf. 20:2, 4, 6); the text does not add “and humiliated her” (34:2) or “and went in to her” (38:2).

Lot’s separation from Abraham alienates him from blessing. He turns his back on his uncle and ignores the dangers of Sodom. But “even as he thought he was living in heaven, he had already sunk almost into hell” (Calvin, _Commentary_ on Gen. 13:10). In contrast to Lot, Abraham trusts God and by faith inherits “all the land ... forever” (v. 15) and “offspring as the dust” (v. 16).
The Hebrew word here is translated “severe” in 12:10, inviting a contrast in Abraham’s situation before and after he went to Egypt (12:10–20 note).
Paradoxically, God’s blessing, not famine, provokes the problem (v. 10 note).

Lot and Abraham are compared and contrasted: both look around (vv. 10, 14), are offered land (vv. 9, 15–17), and travel to their allotted portion (vv. 11–12, 18). But Lot, who chooses by sight, will escape twice by the skin of his teeth (14:12, 16; 19:1–29), while by faith Abraham will be enriched forever.
Faith in God’s sovereignty gives Abraham the freedom to be generous (cf. 14:19, 20). God applauds generosity and peacemakers (Lev. 19:18; Ps. 133; Matt. 5:43–48; James 3:17, 18).

The edge of the Promised Land or just beyond it (Num. 34:2–12); this area is contrasted with Canaan in v. 12.

**like the garden of the** LORD. Humanity’s environment is not the cause of sin—human depravity is. In the ideal environment of Eden sin originated, and sin now abounds in the rich territory that Lot chooses (v. 13; 18:16–19:29).
See note on 14:12.

The Lord invited Moses to a similar panoramic overview of the land (Deut. 34:1–4). In each case, the invitation is given to confirm the promise to one who will not participate in dispossessing the Canaanites.

See 12:1 and note. The promises of land were fulfilled several times but never consummated. God fulfilled the promise through Joshua (Josh. 21:43–45) but not completely (Josh. 13:1–7); even more so through David and Solomon (1 Kin. 4:20–25; Neh. 9:8) but still not completely (Ps. 95:11; Heb. 4:6–8; 11:39–40; Heb. 12:22–24). As Israel’s exodus from Egypt through the Passover (Ex. 12:1) is a type of the church’s exodus from bondage to sin through Christ (1 Cor. 5:7; 10:1–4), so also old Israel’s life in the land is a type of new Israel’s life in Christ. Both are a gift (15:7, 18; Deut. 1:8; Rom. 6:23) and are received by faith (Num. 14:26–44; Josh. 7 and John 3:16). Both uniquely possess the blessed presence, life, and rest of God (Ex. 23:20–31; Deut. 11:12; 12:9,10; 28:1–14; John 1:51; 14:9; Matt. 11:28), and demand persevering faith (Deut. 28:15–19; Heb. 6). The land promises are consummated forever in the new heaven and new earth (Heb. 11:39, 40; Rev. 21:1–22:6).

See 32:12. The promise of offspring also finds fulfillment in old Israel (Num. 23:10; 1 Kin. 4:20; 2 Chr. 1:9) and consummation in the new Israel, composed of Jew and Gentile (12:3 and note; Rom. 4:16–18; Gal. 3:29; Rev. 7:9).

According to ancient custom, a property transfer was finalized by the new owner’s visit to the tract. By this command, God has Abraham lay symbolic claim to the Promised Land (12:7 and note; Josh. 1:3; 18:4; 24:3).

See note on 12:6.

**Mamre.** An Amorite who will seek security in an alliance with Abraham (14:13) and be blessed through him (14:24).

**built an altar.** See 12:7 and note.

Abraham displays obedient faith by risking his life to deliver his nephew, Lot. His victory is astonishing since the plundering confederacy of five kings has just conquered many Canaanites and a confederacy of five Dead Sea kings. See note on v. 4.

**14:1, 2** None of these kings has been definitely identified in extrabiblical sources. One comes from Elam (part of modern Iran), one from Babylon (part of modern Iraq), and two probably from the region of modern Turkey.

**14:1 Shinar.** See note on 10:10.
They are subject as vassals to the king of Elam with the obligation to pay him tribute.
See note on Deut. 2:10–12. The mention of these defeated nations further emphasizes the impressiveness of Abraham’s victory.
See note on Deut. 2:10–12.
Note the progressive identification of Lot with Sodom: camping near it (13:12), living in it, and residing as a respected citizen in it (19:1, 6).

Probably an ethnic identification designating Abraham as a descendant of Eber (10:21 note). However, some contend that the term derives from _habiru,_ a disparaging word used to designate a widely dispersed social class of semi-nomads in the ancient Near East of the second millennium B.C.

**oaks of Mamre.** See note on 12:6.

**Amorite.** Sometimes a blanket term for the earlier inhabitants of Palestine (48:22; Deut. 1:44; Josh. 2:10). Mamre the Amorite, an ally of Abraham who accompanies him in battle, finds blessing through his identification with Abraham (v. 24; cf. 12:3).

The term explains the character of Abraham’s action: the godly display of loving loyalty toward his nephew.

**trained men.** Servants trained in the use of weapons. A fighting force of three hundred men was a sizable army in Abraham’s time.

**Dan.** This place name was updated from Laish after the time of Moses (see Introduction: Date and Occasion; Judg. 18:29).

Lit. “king of righteousness.” The Hebrew word _melek_ means “king,” and _tsedek_ means “righteousness.” See Introduction: Christ in Genesis; Heb. 7:1–3 and notes.

**king of Salem ... priest of God.** The introduction of Melchizedek emphasizes that he is a king as well as a priest. This remarkable priest-king associated with Jerusalem is mentioned in the book of Hebrews to explain how Jesus can also be a priest-king in spite of not being a Levite (cf. Ps. 110:4). Salem was apparently an ancient name for Jerusalem (Ps. 76:2).

**bread and wine.** The combination means “a full dinner, a banquet.”

That Melchizedek blesses Abraham is understood by the author of Hebrews to indicate that Melchizedek is greater than Abraham (Heb. 7:1–8).

**God Most High.** Hebrew _El Elyon._ Similar titles are used of God in the Genesis narrative (e.g., _El Olam,_ “Everlasting God”). The patriarchs used these titles for the Lord, the true God, creator of heaven and earth. Abraham interprets Melchizedek’s praise in this way, repeating the same titles but adding the covenantal divine name LORD (Yahweh) in v. 22. Though probably a Canaanite, Melchizedek knows the true God—a pagan priest cannot meaningfully “bless” Abraham, nor can Abraham, who is consecrating the land to the Lord (12:7 note), give “a tithe” to the priest of the depraved Canaanite god El.

The practice of paying a tenth to a king or to a god was widespread in the ancient Near East, and predates the Mosaic law (28:22; Lev. 27:30–33; Num. 18:21–32). Abraham’s gift to Melchizedek is probably not the payment of the “king’s tithe” (cf. 1 Sam. 8:15, 17) but rather an offering that reflects Abraham’s regard for Melchizedek as a priest of the true God. By giving this tenth to Melchizedek, Abraham affirms his agreement with what Melchizedek has said in blessing God for the victory.

**everything.** The booty won in battle against the four kings.
LORD. See note on v. 19.

In contrast to his dealings with Melchizedek, from whom he accepted bread and wine (v. 18) and to whom he gave a tithe (v. 20), Abraham wants nothing to do with the wicked king of Sodom. Abraham rejects the use of military force in order to take control of the land of Canaan. He will wait for God to give it to him.
The spoil is their rightful share. Abraham’s disposition towards the goods emphasizes his fairness and generosity.

After Abraham’s expression of faith in God’s reward (14:22, 23), God certifies His promise of offspring (vv. 1–6) and land (12:7 and note) by making a covenant (vv. 18–21; Neh. 9:8). The two night scenes (vv. 5, 17) parallel each other: the Lord promises a reward (vv. 1, 7); Abraham questions the sovereign Lord about the inheritance (vv. 2–3, 8); and the Lord responds with a visual act (vv. 4–5, 9–21). Abraham’s faith is accounted to him as righteousness (v. 6).

**15:1 word of the** LORD **came.** This phrase typically introduces a revelation to a prophet (20:7 note; Jer. 18:1; Ezek. 6:1; Hos. 1:1).

**vision.** Visions were an ancient mode of revelation (Num. 12:6) and often occurred at night (v. 5; 1 Sam. 3:1–3; Job 33:14–16).

**reward.** See note on 14:23.

This Hebrew metaphor may mean either “to live childless” or “to die childless.” Abraham is perplexed, perhaps in part because childlessness is seen in his day as a sign of divine judgment (Lev. 20:20, 21; 1 Sam. 1:11; Jer. 22:30) but more likely because God’s promise of nationhood requires descendants.

verse_quote: a member of my household ... heir.
note: The practice of a childless couple adopting a slave as heir is attested in the Nuzi texts (c. 1500 B.C.), a collection of over four thousand clay tablets found near Kirkuk in modern Iraq.
See 12:7; 13:16 and notes.

This verse provides the early core doctrine of justification by faith apart from works (Gal. 3:6–14). Abraham believes the promise of the birth even though, humanly speaking, he is “as good as dead” and not likely to produce an heir with Sarah (Rom. 4:17–21; Heb. 11:11, 12). By faith alone God counts Abraham as righteous. Abraham’s justification by faith is a model of our faith in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, God’s sacrifice for sin, and God’s crediting Christ’s righteousness to us by faith alone (Rom. 4:22–25).

**believed.** Abraham is father of all who believe (Rom. 4:11), and all who believe are children of Abraham (Gal. 3:7).

**righteousness.** See 6:9 and note; Heb. 11:6–12.

LORD **who brought you out.** A portent of God’s self-identification after the exodus (Ex. 20:2).

**land.** See note on 13:15.
His request for a sign is motivated by faith (v. 6; cf. Is. 7:10–14).
All the species that are suitable for sacrifice.

Symbolic of the unclean nations seeking to destroy the descendants of Abraham.

**drove them away.** Abraham symbolically defends his promised inheritance against foreign attackers.
Israel must inherit Canaan through God’s supernatural act of redemption from slavery.
A round number for the period spent in Egypt (cf. Ex. 12:40, 41).
See note on 14:13.

verse_quote: smoking fire pot and a flaming torch.
note:
Symbols of God’s presence with Israel on its way to the Promised Land (cf. Ex. 13:21; 19:18; 20:18).

**passed between these pieces.** As other ancient Near Eastern texts and Jer. 34:18 indicate, by passing between the torn animals (signifying the punishment due those who break the covenant) God invokes a self-maledictory oath or curse upon Himself should He fail to keep His covenant. Because He can swear by no higher authority, God swears by Himself to keep the covenantal terms. See 22:16, 17; Heb. 6:13 note.

God’s covenant with Abraham closely parallels ancient Near Eastern royal land grants made by kings to loyal servants and their descendants in perpetuity. See theological note “Covenant” on previous page.

**from the river ... Euphrates.** Delineation of borders was an important part of the ancient royal land grants.

**river of Egypt.** It is debated whether the brook of Egypt, the Wadi el Arish in northeastern Sinai (Num. 34:5), or the eastern branch of the Nile delta is in view. See 1 Kin. 4:21.
In addition to its geographical boundaries the land is defined by its occupants. See 10:15–18.

In her impatience, Sarah tries to fulfill the divine promise through her own initiative by means of her maidservant, Hagar. The immediate result is strife in the home, and its long-term consequence is the mixed blessing of numerous progeny who will inherit Hagar’s defiant spirit (v. 12). This natural generation will not bring peace; only the greater seed of Abraham (Gal. 3:16), the Son of the God of peace, can do that.

**16:1 servant.** The Hebrew term denotes a personal servant of the wife, not a slave girl (cf. 21:10 note). Her relationship to Sarah resembles Eliezer’s to Abraham (15:2).
In this custom, attested so far in the Code of Hammurabi and in texts from Nuzi and Nimrud, the authority over the children resulting from this union belonged to the chief wife, not the slave-wife.
The Hebrew word here is translated “curse” in 12:3 (12:3 note; cf. Prov. 30:23). Because she treats Sarah with disdain, Hagar is alienated from the family of blessing.

verse_quote: May the wrong done to me be on you.
note:
Sarah lays responsibility for the situation upon Abraham. The narrative suggests that all parties share responsibility for the tense situation that develops.

**May the** LORD **judge.** She appeals to a still higher court (31:53; Ex. 5:21; 1 Sam. 24:12, 15).

According to the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1750), the despised mistress in this situation could not sell her maidservant, but she could mark her with the slave mark and count her among the slaves.

**dealt harshly ... fled.** The intractable Ishmael is the unruly son of a mother who chooses the freedom of the wilderness over submitting to the yoke of her mistress (v. 9).

LORD. The identity of the angel of the Lord is debated. According to some scholars, the angel of the Lord appears in many instances to be a theophany, a visual manifestation of God Himself (e.g., 18:1–33; 22:11–18; 32:24–30; Ex. 3:2–6), though the angel of the Lord is sometimes distinguished from God in other cases (e.g., 21:17). Hagar’s remarks in v. 13 imply that she has seen God. Others, however, note that “angel” means “messenger.” They argue that as secular messengers are fully equated with their senders (Judg. 11:13; 2 Sam. 3:12, 13; 1 Kin. 20:2–4), so God’s angel is identified with Him (see also Gen. 21:17; 31:11; Ex. 14:19; 23:20; 32:34). Either way, God communicates to Hagar through the angel in this text.

**Shur.** The name means “wall,” a reference to Egyptian border forts. Hagar apparently flees toward her home in Egypt (cf. v. 1).
See notes on 3:9 and 11:5.

Abraham fathers many descendants. It is not the mere natural children who finally inherit the promise (Rom. 9:8). Even the physical offspring of Abraham may persecute the sons of promise (21:9; Gal. 4:29, 30).
The fierce, aggressive ways of the Ishmaelites will leave a legacy of conflict.

verse_quote: You are a God of seeing.
note: This divine name is not attested elsewhere. It expresses the deep significance to Hagar of God’s gracious revelation to her. Even while she is lost in the wilderness, God sees her and reveals Himself to her.

verse_quote: it lies between Kadesh and Bered.
note: Today the site is uncertain.

Ishmael’s genealogy is given in 25:12–18. Abraham may view him as the son through whom God will fulfill His purposes (cf. 17:18), especially given that God’s intervention causes Hagar to return to Abraham’s household. However, God promises Abraham another son through whom the promises will be fulfilled: Isaac (cf. v. 19).

See text note. This divine name may signify God’s universal dominion. It occurs frequently in Job, as well as in the patriarchal narratives, often when the covenant promise of progeny is stressed (28:3; 35:11; 43:14; 48:3; 49:25).

**walk before me, and be blameless.** These phrases denote the service due a king. Even Israel’s kings were commanded to “walk before” their greater sovereign, the Lord Himself (1 Kin. 9:4; 2 Kin. 20:3). The covenantal arrangement again surfaces: God’s gracious promises call for the obedient response of Abraham.

The covenant relationship between God and Abraham includes both promises obligating God to Abraham (vv. 4–8, 16) and commands obligating Abraham and Sarah to God (“As for you,” vv. 9–15). This pattern of mutual obligation is not a relationship of equal parties (as in a human contract). Rather, God sovereignly bestows the covenant, gives the grace of faith and obedience to the elect, and graciously provides the remedy for human disobedience (28:20 note). The history of the covenant of circumcision in the OT is largely one of human failure fully to obey the covenantal requirements. Nevertheless, the gracious covenant God remains faithful to His promises even when human beings are faithless (v. 7 note; Lev. 26:44, 45; Deut. 4:30, 31; 2 Tim. 2:13 and note).

Abram, an ancient West Semitic name, means “exalted father,” perhaps originally a reference to Abraham’s father Terah. “Abraham” sounds like a Hebrew expression meaning “father of a multitude of nations.” His old name spoke of his aristocratic ancestry; the new speaks of his many offspring.

**your name shall be.** The name changes of the patriarch and matriarch show that they are under God’s rule (1:5 note) and are called to a new destiny and mission.

**father of a multitude of nations.** Abraham is the physical father of several nations: ethnic Israel through the promised son Isaac, the Ishmaelites through his son Ishmael (v. 20; 21:13; 25:12–18), the Edomites through his grandson Esau (25:23; 36:1–43), and his descendants through Keturah (25:1–4). But this promise finds final fulfillment in the multitude of people from every tribe, language, and nation who share the faith of Abraham and are baptized into Jesus Christ (Rom. 4:16, 17; 15:8–12; Gal. 3:29; Rev. 7:9). The term “father” need not imply a biological connection. Later, Joseph describes himself as “a father to Pharaoh” (45:8).

The descendants of Abraham through the child of promise, Isaac (Rom. 4:19; 9:6–9). Gentile believers participate in this covenant promise through spiritual incorporation into Israel (Eph. 2:11–13; 1 Pet. 2:10 note) by union with Christ, the great offspring (seed) of Abraham (Gal. 3:16, 26–29).

**everlasting.** The unilateral and gracious nature of God’s covenant with Abraham is underscored by its _eternal_ character (v. 2 note). God’s covenant endures forever because He does not change, and Jesus Christ fulfills the covenant’s every condition (2 Cor. 1:20; Eph. 2:12, 13).

**to be God to you.** Although there is a legal dimension to the covenant (v. 2 note), God’s covenant relationship with His people is also one of divine-human communion and fellowship (Ex. 6:7; Deut. 29:13). God graciously dwells with His people, and they gratefully respond in faith, love, and obedience.
See 13:15 and note.

By the ritual of circumcision, old covenant believers consecrated the organ of procreation to God. This draws attention to the concept of “seed” or “offspring,” recalling the importance of the seed of the woman (3:15; 4:25). More importantly, God has always wanted the heart consecrated to Him (Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; 6:10; Ezek. 44:7, 9). Mere circumcision in the flesh is inadequate to please God (17:11–14 notes; Jer. 9:25, 26).
See note on 9:12.

See Luke 1:59; 2:21; Phil. 3:5. Some ancient Near Eastern cultures circumcised their children at puberty as a rite of passage from childhood to manhood. God employed the sign for infants to show that the children of believing parents are “holy” (i.e., separated from the profane world and members of the covenant community, Rom. 11:16; 1 Cor. 7:14). God continues to use the family institution (Acts 16:31). The initiation rite into the covenant community today is baptism. In Christ there is no longer male or female, Jew or Gentile, so all may come (Gal. 3:26–29; Col. 2:11, 12). See theological note “Infant Baptism.”

The covenant promises are extended to all within the household of faith. Even in the OT, the scope of the covenant community was not exclusively determined by ancestry—a foreshadowing of the expansion of the covenant to a multitude from every tribe and nation. See notes on vv. 6, 7.

**in your flesh an everlasting covenant.** See note on v. 7. The covenant of grace between God and His people is indeed an eternal covenant, although the mode of administration changes with the transition from Israel to the church (e.g., circumcision is replaced by baptism, see v. 12 note). See “The Sacraments” at Matt. 28:19.

verse_quote: who is not circumcised ... shall be cut off.
note: Circumcision, the sign of inclusion into the covenant community, also bore associations with death and judgment (i.e., “cutting off”). Though it may seem strange that God would choose a judgment symbol as an entrance rite associated with the covenant of promise, this act points toward the sacrifice of Christ, who experienced divine judgment in order to bring sinners into a covenant relationship of fellowship and peace with God.

See text note. Both names seem to be variants meaning “princess.” Her birth name probably looks back on her noble descent, whereas her covenant name looks ahead to her noble descendants (v. 5 and note).
See note on 12:2.
See note on 21:3.

By His own sovereign counsel the Lord chooses Isaac, not Ishmael (see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Isaac’s unexpected birth signifies that the people of God result not from mere natural generation, but from the promise and the supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit (Rom. 4:17; Gal. 4:21–31). An important distinction is drawn between the unique family line that will eventually lead to Jesus Christ and all those who are circumcised, which includes Ishmael and all the males within Abraham’s household. The former are the source of blessing, whereas the latter are its recipients.
Abraham demonstrates his faith in God’s gracious covenant promises by his obedience (v. 1 note; Rom. 4:9–12).

See note on 12:7.

**oaks of Mamre.** See note on 12:6.

**heat of the day.** The time when travelers seek shade and rest.

The Lord and two angels (vv. 1, 13; 19:1). The NT admonition to show hospitality in Heb. 13:2 is based on the incidents in chs. 18 and 19.

**ran.** Observing the ancient Near Eastern custom of hospitality, Abraham typifies the gracious host and is completely at the service of his guests. His behavior contrasts with the immorality of the Sodomites (19:4, 5).
This Hebrew term unequivocally refers to God.
See notes on 3:9 and 11:5.

verse_quote: The way of women had ceased to be.
note: Lit. “Sarah no longer experienced the cycle of women.” Her body is no longer able to conceive (Heb. 11:11, 12; Rom. 4:19).
Despite her initial skepticism, Sarah will also come to believe the promise (Heb. 11:11) and join her husband in faith (Rom. 4:13–25).
See note on 21:3.

The Lord’s promise of a miraculous offspring anticipates that Abraham will become a great and powerful nation to bless the earth. Beginning with its father, Abraham, such a nation must learn justice (vv. 17–19). The Lord demonstrates His justice to Abraham in the judgment upon the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 20–33). God investigates the accusations thoroughly (vv. 20–21; 11:5 note), and he promises to spare the city even if he can find only ten righteous people there (v. 32).

God so esteems Abraham that He reveals His plans to him. This may be one of the grounds for considering him a prophet (20:7; Amos 3:7; cf. John 15:15). As a prophet, Abraham also intercedes for others (cf. Jer. 15:1; 27:18; Amos 7:1–9).

verse_quote: I have chosen him, that he may.
note:
The Hebrew word translated “chosen” here means “chosen in love.” The purpose of God’s sovereign and gracious election is that His people will be holy and righteous in His sight (Eph. 1:4).

**that the** LORD **... what he has promised.** Those promises claimed by Abraham in faith must be claimed by his descendants as well. Their hope in God’s covenant will be demonstrated by their covenant obedience. God’s plan will be realized through the covenant faithfulness of His people (22:18; 26:4, 5). See note on 17:2.

All cries of wrongdoing come to the attention of the “Judge of all the earth” (v. 25; cf. 4:10). Despite the mercy shown to Sodom through Abraham (ch. 14), Sodom has not repented of its sin.

**their sin.** The sinfulness of Sodom is both proverbial and extensive (13:13; Jer. 23:14). It involves extreme displays of sexual depravity (particularly homosexuality, 19:5; Jude 7), arrogance and abuse of the poor (Ezek. 16:49, 50), and a failure to show hospitality (19:8).
See note on 11:5.

verse_quote: Will you indeed sweep away the righteous.
note: Clearly, no one can escape the massive destruction intended for the cities, so Abraham petitions God on behalf of the righteous who might reside there. The series of questions and answers that follow establish beyond doubt the justice of God’s judgment.

God’s mercy is evident in His willingness to spare the sinful majority for the sake of even ten righteous people. Fewer than ten can be saved individually, as happens in ch. 19. In cases of special punishment inflicted upon cities and nations, righteous individuals were sometimes singled out for preservation (Josh. 6:25; cf. Ezek. 14:14, 16, 18, 20).

Just as God had rescued righteous Noah from the sinful pre-flood world (chs. 6–8), so also He rescues Lot from Sodom. Ultimately, Lot is saved because of God’s mercy to him (v. 16) and because of God’s covenantal commitment to Abraham (v. 29). The destruction of Sodom becomes a paradigm of God’s judgment on sin (Is. 1:9, 10; Ezek. 16:46–49; Amos 4:11; Rom. 9:29; 2 Pet. 2:5, 6).

**19:1–11** See the similar episode recorded in Judg. 19:15–25.

**19:1 two angels.** See note on 18:2. The two angels continue on to Sodom, but the Lord Himself does not appear after 18:33; He will rain down the judgment from heaven (v. 24).

**sitting in the gate.** See 14:12 and note. That Lot was sitting in the city gate indicates his status as a respected member of the community. However, as vv. 6–9 reveal, he is clearly powerless to stop the sinful actions of his fellow citizens. In that ancient culture, legal matters were decided at the city gate by community elders such as Lot (Deut. 21:18–21; Amos 5:15).

**bowed himself.** Throughout the story Lot demonstrates his righteousness by his hospitality to strangers (cf. 2 Pet. 2:6, 7). His actions parallel those of Abraham (18:2 and notes).

verse_quote: young and old ... to the last man.
note: These details are necessary to show that everyone destroyed was wicked (18:23 note). See also 6:5; 8:21; Rom. 1:26–32.
The character of Lot’s appeal demonstrates his righteousness (2 Pet. 2:6, 7).

See notes on 18:2 and 19:1. As one bound by the ancient Near Eastern code of hospitality, which required the protection of guests, Lot is willing to risk danger to his own family rather than allow harm to come to his guests.
See note on 7:16.

The account of Isaac is one of tension between Isaac and Rebekah (v. 28; ch. 27), Jacob and Esau (25:19–34; chs. 27; 32; 33), Jacob and Laban (chs. 29–31), Leah and Rachel (29:31–30:24), and finally and decisively between Jacob and the angel of the Lord (32:22–32; cf. 16:7 note). At the story’s core is the promise to Abraham (24:7), passed on to Isaac and Jacob (26:2–5; 28:3, 4, 13–15; 35:11–12). The promise is elaborated to include God’s protective presence (28:15; 31:42; 32:9, 12; 35:3). Overarching the entire story is God’s sovereign good pleasure (Rom. 9:10–12). He opens Rebekah’s barren womb, announcing the supremacy of Jacob over Esau. In the subsequent narrative, God’s purposes are fulfilled in spite of obstacles placed in the way by human participants.

**26:34, 35** The story of the stolen blessing is framed by references to Esau’s marriage to Hittite women and his parents’ resulting displeasure (27:46). Profane Esau shows his disregard for the covenant blessings by marrying daughters of the land (24:3–4; 31:50 and notes). By intermarrying with the Canaanites and so vexing his parents (27:46), he effectively seals himself off from the sacred inheritance (21:21; 25:6).

**26:34 Hittite.** See note on 10:15.

verse_quote: delicious food, such as I love.

**27:5 Rebekah was listening.** In keeping with a long-standing pattern, Isaac neither provides spiritual leadership in the home nor does he listen to his wife’s counsel—factors that strongly contribute to his family difficulties. Isaac’s behavior contrasts with that of Abraham (21:8–14).

Isaac fails because he depends on his fallible senses—touch (v. 22), taste (v. 25), and smell (v. 27)—rather than upon spiritual understanding (v. 4 note; cf. 13:8–17 note).

This physical contact was part of the ancient blessing ritual (48:1 note).

**27:29 Cursed be everyone who curses.** See 12:3.
See Heb. 12:16, 17 and notes.
See text note; note on 25:26.

While God will give to Jacob “of the dew” and “of the fatness” (v. 28), Esau will dwell “away from the fatness of the earth” and “away from the dew of heaven.” This blessing will find fulfillment as Esau’s descendants, the Edomites, settle in the arid region southeast of the Dead Sea. See note 25:23. From time to time Edom was able to break free of Israelite domination (2 Kin. 8:20–22). In addition, Herod the Great was a descendant of Esau.

**Rebekah said.** As Sarah took initiative to provide for Isaac (21:10), here Rebekah acts for Jacob.

**the Hittite women.** See 26:34 and note on 10:15.

The negative and positive commands correspond to those of Abraham (24:3–4).

**28:1 blessed.** See note on 27:7. The first blessing (27:27–29) determined the patriarchal succession; this one explicitly links Jacob with the blessings of the Abrahamic covenant (17:1–8).

**28:2 Paddan-aram.** See note on 25:20.

See note on 17:1.

The Lord appears to Jacob and gives him promises at critical points in his life: during his flight to Paddan-aram (28:10–22) and on his return to confront Esau (31:3; 32:1, 2, 22–32).

Jacob names the place Bethel to underline this connection, anticipating a time in the future when God’s presence will fill the earth. Jacob’s dream of a meeting place between heaven and earth also points forward to Jesus Christ, the God-man who reunites heaven and earth (John 1:51 and note). Through Christ, the only “mediator between God and men” (1 Tim. 2:5), we have access to the Father (Eph. 2:18).

LORD **stood above it.** Or, “the LORD stood beside him.” If this second reading is preferred (note Jacob’s response in v. 16: “Surely the LORD is in this place”), then God comes down the stairway in Jacob’s dream. He does not stand above the stairway, but over a sleeping Jacob.

**land on which you lie.** God’s promise is adapted to the immediate situation.

A witness and monument drawing attention to the importance of the place (cf. 31:45–59).

The longest vow recorded in the OT.

Note that God’s unconditional promises of vv. 13–15 are here transformed into a conditional bargain: if God does His part, then Jacob will acknowledge Him as God (v. 21). God had sovereignly chosen Jacob in the womb (25:23 and note), and now He graciously bestows the patriarchal promise quite apart from Jacob’s faith; that, too, must be the gift of God (17:2 note; Eph. 2:8-9).
See note on 14:20.

Jacob experiences the blessings of divine providence in meeting Rachel (vv. 1–14), and in a bitter irony the deceiver becomes the deceived (vv. 15–29). Behind the two scenes, the gracious and just hand of the sovereign God, who works all things according to His own purpose and who promised to be with Jacob (28:15), can be discerned.

The similarity of this meeting at the well with the meeting in 24:11–33 suggests the benevolence of divine providence but also highlights the contrast between the prayerful servant and the prayerless patriarch.
The greeting is a gesture of goodwill.

The stone is large (v. 2). Earlier the gold jewelry of Abraham’s servant had attracted Laban’s attention (24:30); now Jacob’s feat of strength impresses Laban with the kind of service Jacob could render.
A customary greeting among relatives (v. 14; 31:55).
The name Rachel means “ewe,” while Leah perhaps means “wild cow” or “wild ox.”

As Jacob took advantage of his father’s blindness to deceive him, so Laban uses the cover of night to outwit Jacob.

**he took his daughter Leah.** The custom of veiling the bride (24:64, 65 note) and of marrying off the elder daughter first (v. 26) serve Laban’s selfish intentions. He shamelessly uses his unloved daughter and introduces a source of continuing discord into Jacob’s family (30:1, 2; 31:15). Laban’s daughters are not deceived by his unscrupulous behavior (31:14–16).

This statement underscores the irony of Jacob’s situation. Jacob has stolen the blessing customarily reserved for the firstborn (ch. 27), and here Laban deceives Jacob in order to uphold a similar custom.
The week of bridal feasting. The extended feast (v. 22) celebrates Laban’s cleverness and Jacob’s humiliation, turning what should be a joyous occasion into a bad joke.

God blesses Jacob with twelve sons in spite of his prayerlessness and the rivalry of Rachel and Leah, who compete for his affections by bearing him sons (25:19–35:29 note). The names the mothers give these children reflect this struggle and also their recognition of God’s assistance to them in their unloved or childless states. God will graciously build up Israel by championing the needy (e.g., Hannah in 1 Sam. 1), but the spiritual failures of Jacob’s family will later result in rivalries among Israelite tribes.

**29:31–35** God graciously gives Leah, the unloved wife, half of Jacob’s sons, including the priestly line of Levi (v. 34) and the messianic line of Judah (v. 35; 49:10). The first and last of the children born in Paddan-aram are given by the Lord to compensate disgraced wives, first Leah (v. 32), then Rachel (30:23, 24).

**29:31 opened.** See 16:2; 20:17, 18.

**barren.** See 11:30; 25:21.
The name means “praised,” here of the Lord, and in 49:8 of Judah himself.
A hyperbolic expression of her extreme distress (25:32; 27:46). Ironically, she later dies in childbirth (35:16–18).

verse_quote: Am I in the place of God.
note: Jacob’s angry retort contrasts sharply with the fervent prayer of Isaac for his childless wife (25:21).

See 16:1, 2 and notes.

**on my behalf.** Literally, “on my knees.” The knee was symbolic of parental care (48:12; 50:23; Job 3:12). According to ancient Near Eastern custom, the delivery of the concubine’s child upon the knees of the wife symbolized the adoption of the child by the wife.
Sometimes called “love apples,” the roots of the mandrake plant were considered an aphrodisiac by the ancients and used to promote sexual activity and conception (cf. Song 7:13).
A dowry.
Because Dinah figures prominently in ch. 34, she is the only daughter of Jacob whose name is given (cf. 46:7).
See note on 8:1. This verse is the climax of 29:31–30:24. Rachel credits the birth of Joseph not to the aphrodisiac (v. 14 note) but to God (v. 23).

God sovereignly blesses Jacob’s flocks at Laban’s expense in spite of the inexcusable cunning of both men. Jacob appears to outwit Laban, repaying Laban’s trickery, but he obtains his family and wealth entirely by God’s grace (29:31–30:24; 31:9).

A formula of courtesy in negotiations.

**learned by divination.** Many ancient extrabiblical texts from Mesopotamia pertain to the practice of occult divination, something forbidden in Israel (Deut. 18:10, 14). Noting Jacob’s good fortune, the pagan Laban has attempted to discover the reason through divination (31:19 and note).

**blessed me because of you.** Once again, others are blessed through their association with the patriarchs (12:2, 3; 13:5, 6; 14:13 and note). This anticipates the greater blessing that will come through Jesus Christ.
The opportunistic Laban is reluctant to let Jacob go, for he hopes to receive God’s blessing.

In the ancient Near East, many lambs were white and most goats black or dark brown. Thinking the agreement poses little risk to himself, Laban eagerly grants Jacob’s request for the unusually colored animals (v. 34). Even though Jacob’s scheming denies God His rightful praise, God’s intention to bless Jacob is not thwarted (31:11, 12).
The unscrupulous Laban immediately resorts to cheating. According to the agreement, the unusually colored animals should be Jacob’s starting flock (v. 32). Jacob begins with none of these.
Jacob’s success is due to God’s grace (31:9–12).
God does abundantly more than Jacob has asked (28:20).

In fulfillment of His promise in 28:15, the Lord leads a chastened Jacob back to the Promised Land with great wealth at Laban’s expense, and over Laban’s opposition (v. 42). God remains faithful to His promises despite Jacob’s scheming and the pagan idolatry in his household (v. 19 and note; 28:20 note).

Having previously fled from Canaan to avoid being killed by Esau, Jacob is now divinely instructed to go back. God’s call comes at a time in his life when he is unsettled by Laban’s attitude toward him.

**I will be with you.** See 28:15 and notes.
Jacob responds to God in prompt obedience (cf. 12:4; 17:23; 22:3).

verse_quote: God of my father has been with me.
note: Acknowledging the Lord’s faithfulness, Jacob is ready to pay his vow (v. 13; 28:20–22 and notes).
See note on 29:10.

Jacob deplores the magnitude of Laban’s dishonesty.

**God did not permit him.** In spite of his own schemes, Jacob recognizes that the Lord has blessed him.
See note on 30:31–34.
Through his dishonest behavior toward Jacob, Laban no longer enjoys God’s blessing (12:3; 27:29).
See note on 16:7.
In bitterness against their dishonest father (vv. 14–15) and in recognition of God’s providence (v. 16), Leah and Rachel decide to follow Jacob.

They resent that their father has squandered the bride price that Jacob gave to him; Rachel and Leah cannot look to their father for financial security in the future. The price paid was Jacob’s labor (29:18, 27).

**devoured our money.** This phrase occurs in similar social contexts in Mesopotamian texts from Nuzi (c. 1500 B.C.). Legally, at least part of the bride price received by a father in return for giving his daughter in marriage was to be given to the daughter.
See note on 25:20.

Small household gods or _teraphim_ were thought to provide protection and were used in divination (30:27 note; Ezek. 21:21; Zech. 10:2). Unlike Sarah and Rebekah, Rachel has not given up her pagan idols or ethics (vv. 34, 35; 35:2). Perhaps Rachel hid the idols before she left Laban so that he could not use them to harm Jacob through divination.
Laban has military superiority (v. 29).
God sovereignly protects Jacob as He did Abraham (12:17; 20:3) and Isaac (26:8 and note).
Again Laban appeals to custom (cf. 29:26), this time complaining that the conventional departure ritual had not been followed (cf. 24:60).

verse_quote: It is in my power to ... harm.
note: See v. 23 and note.

The narrative ridicules the false gods—here the powerless idols are sat on by a woman (v. 35 note; Lev. 15:19–24).

**felt all about.** Trusting in their senses, neither Isaac nor Laban discover the truth (27:18–27 note).
The time of her menstrual period. As in ch. 27, the younger child deceives the father.
According to ancient laws specifying the responsibilities of shepherds, such as those in the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1750 B.C.), Jacob should not have been liable for the loss.

verse_quote: If the God ... on my side.
note:
See 28:15, 20 and notes.

**the Fear of Isaac.** Or, “the Awesome One of Isaac.” See v. 53 and note.

**sent me away empty-handed.** An allusion to one of Laban’s more conspicuous faults—his failure to pay workers their just wages (29:25; 31:7, 41).

verse_quote: all that you see is mine.
note: Laban’s claim shows that Jacob’s fears have been justified (v. 31).
This covenant, or “treaty,” is like the nonaggression treaties Abraham and Isaac made with the Philistines (21:27; 26:28), but unlike the unconditional covenant God made with Abraham (15:8).

Laban is deeply concerned to ensure that the status and security of his daughters will not be undermined by Jacob taking other wives. This prohibition is found commonly in marriage contracts from the ancient Near East.

verse_quote: The God of Abraham ... Nahor ... father.
note:
The pagan Laban apparently regards the God of Abraham as one of the gods of his family. Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, had probably been a moon-worshiper in Ur (11:27 note; Josh. 24:14).

**Fear of his father Isaac.** Not equating the God of Abraham with the God of Nahor, Jacob swears by the “Fear of his father Isaac” (v. 42 note), another name for the God of Abraham.
See 24:60; 27:7; 28:1 and notes.

Jacob again encounters the angels of God whom he had met earlier at Bethel (28:12). These angelic encounters upon leaving and returning to the Promised Land frame Jacob’s experiences with Laban (28:10–22 note) and attest to God’s promise to be with and protect Jacob wherever he goes (28:15).

Faithful to His promise, God has been with Jacob—not only protecting him but also remaking his character. The formerly prayerless and ambitiously deceptive Jacob is now a humble man of prayer (vv. 9–12).

See text note. Jacob may have in mind both his camp and God’s camp, a heavenly shield and escort. As Bethel was the house of God and the gate of heaven (28:17), Mahanaim was God’s camp on earth. Mahanaim later served as a capital for Saul’s son Ishbosheth (2 Sam. 2:8) and as a refuge for David during Absalom’s rebellion (2 Sam. 17:24). Mahanaim was situated east of the Jordan River near the River Jabbok, but its precise location is uncertain.
See 25:25 and note.

Jacob’s humble manner of address toward his brother and former rival suggests that his character change is real (v. 1 note). Like Abraham with Lot (13:8, 9), Jacob does not insist on his covenantal privileges but leaves the matter in God’s hands., 5
Jacob has reason to fear (14:14; 27:40, 41), yet he has survived Laban’s forces with God’s help (31:29 and note).
Jacob’s first recorded prayer (vv. 9–12) stands between the two presents to Esau (vv. 3–8, 13–21). This structure suggests that he trusts God to prosper his two gifts.

A spiritual transformation has taken place in Jacob: he submits to Esau and recognizes his unworthiness before God.

**steadfast love ... faithfulness.** Words often used to describe God’s loyalty to His covenant promises (24:27; Ex. 15:13 note; Pss. 40:11; 61:7). Jacob now identifies himself fully with God’s covenant with Abraham and Isaac, and his faith rests firmly on God’s covenant promises.

verse_quote: make your offspring as the sand.
note: In faith Jacob applies to himself the language of the covenantal promise to Abraham (22:17; cf. 28:14).
The Hebrew here connotes tribute, a gift expressing loyalty to a superior. See notes on 33:3, 4 and 33:11.
Five-hundred-fifty animals was an extravagant gift., 15
Lit. “cover his face,” an expression meaning the covering over of guilt. Jacob is painfully aware that he has sinned against his brother.
In wrestling with Jacob, God appears in human form and deprives Jacob of his natural strength, but Jacob tenaciously clings to God for blessing.
This mysterious man is a theophany, a visible (and in this case tangible) manifestation of God, the Angel of the Lord (16:7 note; Hos. 12:4). The Lord unexpectedly initiates the match.

Though Jacob is apparently a man of considerable strength (29:2, 10), the Angel of the Lord accommodates His strength to Jacob’s.

**touched.** God dislocates Jacob’s hip, the wrestler’s pivot of strength (v. 31). Having previously depended upon his wits and strength, Jacob’s natural powers are now crippled. All his future steps will remind him of his dependence upon divine grace.
See note on 3:9.

See note on 17:6.

**Israel.** See text note. The new name indicates that the patriarch is radically transformed through this encounter with God.

**striven with God.** The “man” is implicitly identified as God Himself (v. 30).

verse_quote: Why is it that you ask.
note: In ancient times, a name was thought to express essential nature as well as identity. The divine name partakes of the sacredness of God’s being (Judg. 13:18) and was to be reverenced (Ex. 20:7). The pagans believed that knowing the name of a god imparted ability to invoke that deity’s power. Here, however, the divine name is withheld (cf. 28:13; Hos. 12:5), showing that the Lord’s revelation of His name is a gracious act of divine initiative, not a response to human effort to invoke and control God.

See text note. Peniel was located on the River Jabbok near the modern Tulul edh-Dhahab. The town was destroyed by Gideon (Judg. 8:8) and later fortified by Jeroboam I (1 Kin. 12:25).

**delivered.** Jacob’s preservation during his “face-to-face” meeting with almighty God anticipates his preservation during his imminent encounter with Esau, a mere human being (cf. v. 11).
The restriction against eating the sciatic tendon, mentioned elsewhere only in extrabiblical Jewish literature, commemorates this significant event in the nation’s history.
See note on 32:6.

Jacob greets Esau as a vassal greets his patron in the ceremony of a royal court, with the deference appropriate to a superior—note the sevenfold obeisance (common practice in ancient Near Eastern court protocol, v. 3), the submissive address of a “servant” (v. 5) to his “lord” (vv. 8, 13), and the presentation of gifts of homage (vv. 10, 11). In contrast, Esau greets Jacob as one brother greets another after a long separation (vv. 4, 9)., 4
As Jacob remembers his troubled history, he confesses God’s unmerited kindness in giving him children (29:31–30:24) and prosperity (30:25–31:55).

See 32:13 and note.

**like seeing the face of God.** As at Peniel, when Jacob saw God’s face by theophany and his life was graciously spared (32:30), so also here he sees the dreaded face of Esau and is graciously received.

Although this refers to Jacob’s gift to Esau (v. 10), it recalls his earlier theft of the paternal blessing in ch. 27. Jacob here offers recompense out of the many blessings God has given him.

**urged ... took.** The reconciliation is sealed by accepting the gift.

Given his intention to travel to Succoth (v. 17), Jacob may have been speaking deceptively, but more probably Esau knows that this was Jacob’s polite way of not contradicting him (cf. 23:11 note). Though reconciled, the brothers will live apart.

This final section of “the account of Isaac” (see Introduction: Outline), like the closing section in “the account of Abraham” (22:20–25:11), records the transition of patriarchies. It is structured according to Jacob’s itinerary back in the land, featuring deaths at various sites (which mark the passage of Isaac’s generation), and important episodes in the “account” such as the sins of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.
Jacob builds his altar at Shechem where Abraham built his first altar in the Promised Land (see 12:6, 7). See also 28:20–22.

The threat to the covenant community at Shechem was severe. Hamor’s proposal would have meant the assimilation of Jacob’s family into the surrounding peoples (vv. 8–10; Num. 25:1–3 note).

The transition from Jacob’s act of worship (33:20) to the depraved behavior of ch. 34 is striking. Instead of residing at Shechem (33:18, 19), perhaps Jacob should have fulfilled his vow at Bethel (28:22; 31:13; 35:1). There is no mention of God in this chapter and no separation from idolatry (35:1–5), a sad commentary on Jacob’s spiritual leadership (35:4 note).

See 9:25; 10:15, 17 and notes.

**saw ... seized ... humiliated.** The precise nature of what Shechem does is open to debate. He may have intercourse with Dinah prior to being betrothed, which would have be unacceptable. It is also likely that he rapes her, since the Hebrew word translated “humiliated” is rendered “violated” in 2 Sam. 13:12, 14, 22, 32. The sequence “saw ... seized” recalls 3:6 and 6:2.
The nation of Israel. This description assumes the later development of the nation from the sons of Israel (cf. 49:28).
See note on ch. 34.
This is not the dowry given by the bride’s family to the groom, but rather a reciprocal gift given by the groom to the bride’s father (24:53; 1 Sam. 18:25).
Jacob reaps the whirlwind; his sons copy his deception (27:35, 36).
Jacob’s sons sacrilegiously empty the holy covenant sign of its religious significance (17:10, 11 and notes) and abuse it for the purpose of inflicting vengeance.

The action of Simeon and Levi is totally unjustified according to the doctrine of retribution. Furthermore, it endangers their households (v. 30). For an evaluation of just how distasteful this act is in their father’s eyes, see Gen. 49:5–7.
By their unbridled, faithless, and rash revenge, Simeon and Levi lose leadership and land in Israel (49:5–7).
Jacob here displays fear, not obedient faith (cf. 35:5).

Jacob’s journey through time, as indicated by births (vv. 16–18), deaths (vv. 8, 19, 20), and genealogies (vv. 23–26), and through space, as indicated by itineraries (vv. 6, 16, 21, 27), is brought to completion because God is with him (v. 3). He returns to pay his vow at Bethel (vv. 1–8), is confirmed as the successor to God’s Abrahamic promises (vv. 9–15), sees his twelve sons safely settled in the Promised Land (vv. 16–26), and is reunited with his father and brother (vv. 27–29).

**35:1 go up to Bethel.** Jacob has a vow to fulfill (28:20–22; 34:1–31 note). God’s revelation at Bethel (vv. 9–13) reiterates the covenant promises to Abraham, who himself had earlier worshiped at Bethel (12:8; 13:3, 4).

Repentance involves renouncing whatever hinders or tarnishes the worship and service of God. The covenant’s primary requirement is exclusive allegiance to the Lord (Ex. 20:3–5; Josh. 24:14; Judg. 10:16).

**foreign gods.** See notes on 31:19; Josh. 24:23.

Jacob recovers his spiritual leadership of the family (30:2 note; 34:1–31 note).

**rings ... ears.** These are amulets associated with pagan worship (cf. v. 2).

**terebinth tree ... near Shechem.** Probably the sacred tree associated with Abraham (12:6 and note).

Jacob finally fulfills his vow to the Lord (28:20–22). By such altar building, the patriarchal family acknowledges the covenant promises and consecrates the Promised Land. Regular worship is crucial if they are to maintain their religious separation from the surrounding Canaanites (ch. 34; Num. 25:1–3 and notes). See 12:7 and note; 13:18; 22:9; 33:20.
She is briefly mentioned in 24:59. Scripture memorializes the death of the aged, faithful nurse of Rebekah rather than the matriarch herself, perhaps because of Rebekah’s deception (ch. 27).

God’s revelation to Jacob after his return from Paddan-aram to Bethel confirms the earlier promises of 28:13, 14. Using language that closely parallels the Abrahamic promises of nations, royalty, and land (17:5–8), God confirms His promises to Israel, the transformed Jacob (32:28), and indirectly to his twelve sons.

**35:9 Paddan-aram.** See note on 25:20.
God’s gracious blessing on all humankind (1:28; 9:1, 7) is focused particularly on the covenant community (28:3; cf. 47:27; Ex. 1:7 note).
See notes on 12:7; 13:15.
This recalls Jacob’s first meeting with the Lord at Bethel (28:13 note).

In this narrative of forgiveness and reconciliation, Joseph presents a model of submission to God’s eternal and benevolent purpose (vv. 5–8). All the evil done to him by his brothers was only part of God’s secret plan designed for the good not only of Joseph but also of his wicked brothers. We learn that “all things work together” to accomplish God’s excellent purpose (Rom. 8:28), not only for us who presently “love God,” but for the “great multitude” that will comprise the everlasting city (Rev. 7:9).

These verses, with Joseph’s repeated affirmation “God sent me” (vv. 5, 7, 8), form the theological heart of the Joseph narrative (cf. 50:19–21; Acts 7:9–14). God oversees the course of human action to achieve His good and set purpose (Acts 2:23; 4:28).

This catalog of sons closes the patriarchal period in Canaan and forms a transition to the exodus from Egypt (Ex. 1:1–7). The list includes the sons and grandsons of Jacob (some of whom were born in Egypt) through his various wives and concubines, although his daughters and granddaughters, except for Dinah (v. 15) and Serah (v. 17), are omitted. Thus the list is designed to culminate in the significant number seventy (v. 27 note) to show both God’s blessing on the family and to anticipate their further expansion into a great nation.

**46:8 who came into Egypt.** This list includes the sons of Benjamin, who were probably born in Egypt (vv. 21, 27), just as the catalog of those born in Paddan-aram (35:23–26) included Benjamin, who was obviously born in Canaan (35:26 note). This name is not included in parallel lists (Num. 26:12–13; 1 Chr. 4:24).
