The total of thirty-three (v. 15 and note), sixteen (v. 18), fourteen (v. 22), and seven (v. 25) comes to seventy. The figure of sixty-six persons probably reflects the omission of Er and Onan (v. 12) and Ephraim and Manasseh (vv. 20, 27).

The covenant family is represented by the symbolic number seventy (vv. 8–27 note), signifying a large and complete number (cf. ch. 10 note; Ex. 24:1; Ps. 90:10). In this group of seventy, the emerging nation of Israel is comprehended.

The Septuagint adds five sons and grandsons of Manasseh and Ephraim at v. 20 and gives a total of seventy-five, a reading followed by Stephen in Acts 7:14. Such variations occasionally occur in the Septuagint, and we don’t always have the information necessary to explain them.

Through Joseph’s wisdom God preserves Israel in Goshen, both physically, by providing food and land (45:10 note), and spiritually, by providing for their isolation from the pagan Egyptians until the exodus (43:32; Num. 25:1–3 and notes). Under Jacob’s blessing on Pharaoh (47:7, 10; cf. 12:2) and Pharaoh’s honoring of Israel (45:17–20; 47:6; cf. 12:3) everyone prospers: Pharaoh gains control of all the property and people in Egypt (47:19–21), the Egyptians hail Joseph as a savior (47:25), and Israel prospers even more than the Egyptians (47:27; Ex. 1:7). This mutual blessing and prosperity contrasts with the situation four hundred years later when another pharaoh exploits Israel and suffers the consequences (Ex. 1:8–14).

Their identity as shepherds will assure Pharaoh that they entertain no social or political ambitions under their brother’s auspices and will help insulate them from intermarriage with the pagan Egyptians (v. 34; 43:32 and notes). The latter threat increased when they possessed property in Egypt (47:11).
The Egyptians also kept animals (47:6; Ex. 9:3, 4); this probably refers to foreign shepherds (43:32 note).

In this remarkable audience with mighty Pharaoh—the greater typically blesses the lesser (14:19 and note)—the aged shepherd patriarch demonstrates his dignity. His blessing is fulfilled in vv. 13–25. Once more, Genesis highlights the important theme of blessing being mediated to others through the unique line of offspring descended from Abraham. Ultimately, this is fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Gal. 3:14).

The Hebrew term denotes a temporary abode, the condition of a resident alien. Jacob describes his own life, and that of his fathers, as a sojourn (21:34; 24:3; 26:3 and notes). Though awaiting the fulfillment of the divine covenant promise of land, their hope extends beyond Canaan to a heavenly and eternal country, to a “city ... whose designer and builder is God” (Heb. 11:10). See notes on 13:15 and Heb. 11:8–10.

**Few and evil.** Jacob does not glory in the number of his years. Though blessed by God and a blessing to others, he has had his share of human failings and afflictions.

Assuming an early date for the exodus from Egypt (see Introduction to Exodus: Special Issues), this designation of the land of Goshen, after Pharaoh Rameses II (c. 1279–1213 B.C.), indicates that the place name was updated after the time of Moses (14:14 note; see Introduction: Date and Occasion).
Joseph brings all the money, land, and people under Pharaoh in exchange for food, thereby preserving the Egyptians.
The Hebrew is uncertain. This reading describes the result of Joseph’s policies—servitude for the people. The people, however, view Joseph not as a tyrant but as a savior (v. 25; cf. 45:7).

Having witnessed God’s faithfulness, by faith Jacob looks beyond his death in Egypt to his burial in the Promised Land.

**47:27 gained possessions ... multiplied greatly.** In fulfillment of the divine promise (46:3 and notes). The independence and prosperity of the Israelites contrasts with the fate of the Egyptians (vv. 13–26 note). This description also provides a link with Ex. 1:7.

Jacob later repeats the command to all his sons in 49:29–32, but Joseph is in charge (48:1 note).

**put your hand under my thigh.** See note on 24:2.
By faith Israel sees his destiny in the Promised Land, not in an embalmed body in the choicest land of Egypt (v. 11; 50:2).

Jacob asks that Joseph confirm his promise (v. 30) with a solemn oath. Likewise, God underscores the surety of His gracious covenant promises with oaths (15:8–21; 22:17; Heb. 6:13, 14 note). For Joseph’s fulfillment of his oath, see 50:1–14.

**bowed himself.** An expression of reverent thanksgiving to God that his last wish will be fulfilled (cf. 1 Kin. 1:47, 48).

Joseph receives the rights of firstborn and the double portion through Jacob’s adoption and elevation of Joseph’s two sons to the status of founding fathers among Israel’s twelve tribes (37:8; 43:3; 1 Chr. 5:2 and notes). The adoption ritual includes Jacob’s statements of authority (vv. 3, 4) and intent to adopt Ephraim and Manasseh (vv. 5–7), legal gestures (vv. 8–12), and words of blessing (vv. 15–16). An ancient text from the city of Ugarit (Ras Shamra) describes a similar adoption of a grandson (c. 1500 B.C.).

See note on 17:1.

**appeared ... blessed me.** God’s direct revelation of the covenant blessing to Jacob empowers him to legitimate Joseph’s two sons as numbered among the twelve (v. 5) and to bless the twelve tribes (48:5–49:28). This preference for Joseph, giving him the double portion, reasserts God’s sovereign prerogative to do as He pleases with Israel (see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

**at Luz.** See 28:19.
Jacob briefly summarizes part of the content of the covenant promises to the patriarchs (12:1–3, 7; 13:14–17; 15:12–21; 17:4–8; 22:15–18; 28:3, 4, 13–15).

The younger (Ephraim) is again preferred before the older (vv. 17–20; 25:23 and note).

**Reuben and Simeon.** The first two sons of Leah are mentioned because they are bypassed to give the double portion to Joseph, Rachel’s firstborn. Reuben loses his rights as firstborn because he defiled his father’s marriage bed (35:22; 43:3 note; 49:3, 4). Likewise, Simeon’s actions against the men of Shechem exclude him (34:1–31).

verse_quote: shall be yours ... name of their brothers.
note: Joseph’s other sons are not adopted by Jacob but will be embraced within the clans of Ephraim and Manasseh. These younger sons of Joseph are probably included in Num. 26:28–37; 1 Chr. 7:14–29.

See note on 25:20.

**Rachel.** Though Leah is buried in the family grave (49:31; cf. 35:16–20), Rachel is honored and memorialized in the double portion given her firstborn.
Identification of the beneficiaries is part of the blessing ritual (v. 1 note). The nearly sightless Jacob (cf. 27:1) carefully identifies the recipients of the irrevocable blessing (27:7 note).
Joseph, who shares his father’s faith, gives the same answer that Jacob gave Esau to a similar question (33:5; cf. 41:51, 52 and note).
Part of the blessing ritual (27:26 and note).

In the blessing, Jacob’s perspective shifts from thanksgiving for God’s covenant faithfulness and miraculous provision (v. 15) to anticipation of God’s faithfulness and blessing on future generations (v. 16).

The one second only to Pharaoh (41:40) humbles himself before the patriarch who mediates God’s promises.

**from his knees.** In the ancient Near East, the knee was symbolic of parental care and, by extension, of adoption (30:3 note).

In the ancient Near East oral statements were accompanied by the correct placement of the right hand, an action that functioned as a legal safeguard. This is also the first instance in Scripture where a blessing is accompanied by the laying on of hands (cf. Ps. 139:5; Matt. 19:13–15).

Joseph is represented in his two sons. Joseph is later blessed without distinguishing his two sons (49:22–26). See note on 27:7.

**before whom my fathers ... walked.** See note on 17:1.

An explanatory notice appended here to the ritual so as not to interrupt the narrative (v. 1 note).

**younger brother shall be greater.** Against social convention, the younger is blessed, as in the divine choices of Isaac over Ishmael (17:18, 19), Jacob over Esau (25:23), and Joseph over Reuben (v. 1 note). God’s sovereign choice overrides the natural ways of men (cf. Is. 55:8, 9). While the line of seed will continue through the tribe of Ephraim, it will later be transferred by God to the tribe of Judah (Ps. 78:67–72).
Jacob’s prophetic blessing is fulfilled after the exodus as Ephraim becomes the dominant Israelite tribe in the northern part of the Promised Land (Deut. 33:17 note).

The Hebrew word translated “mountain slope” (_shechem_) often means “shoulder” or “ridge” and is identical to the place-name “Shechem” (33:19). Some see here a reference to the double portion in the Promised Land that Joseph received through Ephraim and Manasseh (v. 1 note). Others infer that Jacob bequeaths the area of Shechem to Joseph’s descendants (Josh. 24:32), the Shechem where Jacob purchased a tract of land (33:18, 19) and that his sons later conquered (34:25–31).

The blessings of the inspired patriarch prophesy the fate of the twelve tribes descended from his sons, mostly by means of wordplays on their names or comparisons to animals. The names and actions (good or bad) of the twelve sons portend the destiny of the tribes. These prophetic blessings at the end of the patriarchal era are arranged according to the mothers—Leah’s six sons (vv. 3–15), the handmaids’ four (vv. 16–21); and Rachel’s two (vv. 22–27)—and exhibit God’s sovereignty over the nation. These blessings will be expanded in the parallel final blessing of Moses upon Israel that is given on the threshold of Israel’s conquest of the Promised Land (Deut. 33).

**49:1 days to come.** Jacob’s prophecies embrace the entire history of Israel from the conquest and distribution of the land to the reign of the Messiah, Jesus Christ (v. 10 and note). See Num. 24:14; Deut. 31:28, 29; Is. 2:2.

The prophecies about Leah’s first three sons, Reuben, Simeon and Levi, pronounce punishment for crimes and do not use animal comparisons. The sins of the fathers impact future generations (Ex. 20:5).

**49:3 Reuben.** See 29:32; 35:22 and note. A son’s inheritance in the ancient Near East could not be altered by a father’s arbitrary decision, but such changes could be made after serious sexual offenses by the son against the family.
Reuben’s behavior with Jacob’s concubine was reckless and destructive. The Hebrew here connotes pride and presumption (cf. Judg. 9:4; 1 Chr. 5:1, 2).
See 29:33, 34; 34:25 and note.

Sharing an inclination toward destructive anger and cruelty, Simeon and Levi pose a threat to peace (34:25–31). After the exodus from Egypt, the tribe of Simeon declines in importance and is not mentioned in Moses’s blessing (Deut. 33). Simeon’s lack of strength as a tribe is also reflected in the fact that the Simeonites are allotted cities within the territory taken by the tribe of Judah and do not get their own land (Josh. 19:1–9). Similarly, the priestly tribe of Levi is allotted cities.

See 29:35; 43:3 and notes.

**your father’s sons shall bow.** The tribes will bow down to Judah’s descendant David because of his heroic deeds (2 Sam. 5:1–3).

Signifying strength, courage, and boldness (Judg. 14:18; Prov. 28:1), the lion is an apt symbol of the warrior kings of Judah’s Davidic line—a royal line culminating in the conquering Messiah, Jesus Christ (Rev. 5:5).

The scepter symbolizes royal authority. This prophecy is further elaborated and confirmed by the Davidic covenant (2 Sam. 7:16).

**until tribute comes to him.** Lit. “Until Shiloh comes.” The precise meaning of this phrase is debated. Some understand “Shiloh” as a place name (“until Judah’s leadership comes to Shiloh”; cf. Josh. 18:1) or as a reference to tribute (“until tribute is brought to Judah”). According to Ps. 78:67–72, the tribe of Judah, through David, assumes leadership of the nation of Israel after God rejects Shiloh as the location for His temple. Others see Shiloh as a reference to a coming Judahite ruler: “until he comes to whom it belongs” (cf. Ezek. 21:27) or “until Shiloh [possibly a messianic term] comes.” The subsequent mention of dominion over “people” (or “peoples”—the Hebrew noun is plural) points to the final realization of this prophecy in the universal messianic reign of Christ (1 Cor. 15:24–28; Rev. 5:5). God’s plan for humanity to rule and have dominion (1:26–28) is concentrated in Him.

The blessedness of the messianic ruler is represented by wine (a symbol of prosperity, 27:28) and by his beauty (Ps. 45:2–9).

**49:11 donkey’s colt.** See Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:7.

Later failing to drive the Canaanites out of its territory, the tribe of Issachar is apparently willing to trade its liberty for forced labor (cf. Judg. 1:28, 30). Issachar throws off the Canaanite yoke under the leadership of Deborah and Barak (Judg. 5:15).
Or, provide justice for them. See 30:6.
Though small, Dan is dangerous and strikes unexpectedly to overthrow larger foes (Judg. 18). The Danite Samson single-handedly strikes the Philistines with great destruction (Judg. 13–16).
A brief prayer stands in the middle of the oracles.
This verse consists of a play on words (four of the six Hebrew words sound like “Gad”) that points to the constant danger to Gad from its southern and eastern neighbors (Ammon and Moab).
A reference to its fertile land (Deut. 33:24; Josh. 19:24–31). See 30:13.

See 30:24; 48:15–20.

**fruitful.** Barren Rachel will produce the most fruitful tribe (30:2, 22; 41:52).

**run over the wall.** The children of Joseph later seek to increase their territory (Josh. 17:14–18).

Note the striking multiplication of divine names.

**49:24 Stone.** Israel’s sure defense (Deut. 32:4 note).

**49:25 Almighty.** See note on 17:1.

**bless.** The Hebrew root for “bless” is used six times in this verse. These blessings are fertility of land fed by water from heaven above and earth below (1:6–8 and note) and fertility of body (1:22; cf. Num. 24:5–7). Blessings given humankind at creation and later associated especially with Abraham are concentrated on Joseph. Through Joseph, the divine promise to bless the nations is continued (cf. 22:18).
See note on Deut. 33:16.
See 35:18. This tribe will later have a fierce reputation (Judg. 20:14–25; 1 Kin. 12:21; 2 Chr. 14:8; 17:17).

Believing in God’s promises to Abraham and Isaac about the Promised Land (13:15 and note), Jacob arranges for his burial with them in Canaan (49:29–32; cf. 47:29–31). Joseph also instructs his family to bury him in the Promised Land after the exodus (50:24–26; cf. Josh. 24:32). The burial of Jacob in the ancestral cave and Joseph’s determination to be buried in Canaan underscore the covenant family’s solidarity and point forward to the exodus from Egypt. The unity of the family is further emphasized by Joseph’s kind words and provisions for his offending brothers (50:15–21).

**49:29 in the cave.** See ch. 23; 25:9 and notes.

An Egyptian practice designed to preserve the body after death and so to maintain personal identity in the afterlife; embalming was not practiced in Israel. Here the embalming preserves the body for transport back to Canaan.

verse_quote: spoke to the household of Pharaoh.
note: Having just mourned his father’s death (Deut. 34:8 note), Joseph’s appearance is probably unsuitable for an appearance before Pharaoh (cf. 41:14).
The Hebrew verb translated “hewed out” can also mean “purchased” (cf. ch. 23). If the text reading is followed, Joseph simply expresses Jacob’s instructions in words Pharaoh will understand.
The protection given the burial party by Egyptian arms contrasts with the threat of Egyptian chariots during the Mosaic exodus (Ex. 14:9; 15:4, 5).
It is unclear whether Jacob has actually said this or the fearful brothers simply have invented it. In any case, they base their plea for forgiveness on their worship of the same God (v. 17).

verse_quote: am I in the place of God.
note: Joseph recognizes that his captivity has been part of God’s gracious plan to save the covenant family (45:5–8); it is not his place to question God’s wisdom.

verse_quote: you meant evil ... God meant it for good.
note:
A classic statement of God’s sovereign overruling of human history to accomplish His gracious purposes (24:27; 45:5, 7, 8 and notes). See “Providence” at Prov. 16:33.

**that many people should be kept alive.** In Egypt, Canaan, and elsewhere (41:57). Viewed in the light of God’s earlier promise to Abraham that all the nations will be blessed through one of his descendants (22:18), Joseph’s actions prefigure those of Jesus Christ. The salvation provided by Christ, however, extends far beyond feeding people in a time of famine.

See notes on 30:3 and 48:12. Joseph apparently adopted these great-grandchildren.

Machir is an important son of Manasseh who becomes the progenitor of the Gileadites (Num. 26:29; 32:39; Deut. 3:15; Josh. 13:31). His descendants later settle the areas of Gilead and Bashan on the eastern side of the Jordan River (Josh. 17:1).

Like his father, Jacob, on his deathbed (48:21), Joseph expresses firm confidence in God’s covenant promises and His gracious visitation. The Hebrew verb translated “visit” denotes a divine encounter that will change one’s fortunes for good or ill. For other instances of God’s gracious “visitation,” see 21:1 (Abraham and Sarah); Ex. 3:16 and 4:31 (the exodus); Luke 1:68, 78 (the birth of Jesus); and Acts 15:14 (the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles).

**Abraham ... Isaac ... Jacob.** For the first time the three patriarchs are mentioned together; the patriarchal era has passed, but not its hope (Ex. 3:6; Deut. 30:20; 1 Kin. 18:36; 2 Chr. 30:6).

Joseph’s bones will be taken from Egypt by Moses (Ex. 13:19) and later buried at Shechem (Josh. 24:32). Ultimately, he sees his time in Egypt as merely a sojourn. His true home is in God’s blessed presence, which is prefigured in dwelling and burial in the Promised Land.
